notes.body:
This narration belongs to a well-attested hadith found in Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Abu Hurayra, and it carries all the marks of a **hadith qudsi** — a sacred narration in which the Prophet ﷺ reports the direct words of Allah, rather than his own prophetic teaching. In Bukhari's collection, the Prophet ﷺ recounts that the womb (رحم) rose before Allah after creation and held fast to Him, and Allah replied to it, establishing its dignity and its tie to His own name. A second, complementary narration — found in Sunan Abu Dawud and corroborated in al-Hakim's Mustadrak — carries the specific wording closest to what the passage quotes: that Allah said to the womb, شققت لك اسماً من اسمي, meaning He derived a name for it from His own name, linking رحم to الرحمن.

The narration is treated as hadith qudsi in character even where individual collections do not label it as such in their chapter headings. Both versions share the same essential revelation: Allah made the womb a living symbol of His own mercy, naming it from Himself so that every human being who passes through it carries, without knowing it, the first impression of divine love.

Slight differences in wording between collections are normal for hadith qudsi narrations — the meaning is preserved consistently across both.

notes.quote: There is this famous HADEES in which Allah is actually speaking directly to the womb.
etymology: حديث قدسي (sacred hadith): حديث comes from the root ح-د-ث, meaning to occur or to speak — something that happened and was then told. قدسي comes from قُدْس, meaning holiness or divine sanctity. Together, hadith qudsi names a narration whose content originates directly with Allah, even though it travels to us through the Prophet ﷺ rather than through the Quran itself.

شَقَّ (to derive, to split): from the root ش-ق-ق, meaning to cleave or to open something apart. When Allah says He شَقَّ a name from His own name, the image is of something being cut from a living whole — not a copy made at a distance, but a piece drawn directly from the source, so that the derived word carries the life of the original within it.

notes.body:
The passage tells us we are انسان — and the Arabic word carries within it a classical trace: one root scholars point to is نِسْيَان, forgetting. We are not, by nature, creatures of malice; we are **creatures of forgetfulness**, and this single fact unlocks what شریعۃ is for. He gave us a structure woven into every corner of life not from distrust, but because He knows that without it, we will forget.

Look at the rules of punishment in شریعۃ. At first glance, they seem to speak of severity, not love. But consider what they are protecting: life, honour, the family — the very things Allah wrapped around us as expressions of His رحمۃ. **A punishment in sharia is the womb wall** — the boundary a mother's body draws around the child so the outside world cannot reach it before its time.

The laws of contract carry the same mercy into the marketplace. When a deal is written down and witnessed, the person with less power cannot be crushed afterward. When debts are recorded, no one can deny what was agreed. This is Allah saying, through the structure of law: **I have not forgotten the vulnerable**. رحمۃ does not only descend as a feeling from above; it is inscribed into the horizontal ties between people, so that mercy is present even when no one is looking up.

Inheritance law reaches that mercy forward through time. When a person dies, the rules are already in place to ensure that no widow is left without provision and no orphan without a share. Every domain of شریعۃ — the courtroom, the contract table, the division of an estate — is another surface where رحمن keeps showing up. **The whole of law is structured remembrance**: not a reminder to fear Him, but a reminder that He never stopped caring.

notes.quote: All of شریعۃ is just a reminder of that. Because as soon as any decent human being is presented and reminded of the love, care, concern and mercy of another person, he naturally responds with praise and gratitude.
etymology: شریعۃ: from the root ش-ر-ع. Lane's Lexicon gives شَرَعَتِ الدَّوَابُّ فِي الْمَاءِ — the animals entered the water and drank. The شَرِيعَة is the clear path that leads down to the watering place. Law named for a road to water: not a barrier keeping you out, but the way that brings the thirsty to what sustains them.

رحمۃ: from the root ر-ح-م. The رَحِم is the womb — Lane describes it as the place of origin and the receptacle of the young. Every form — رَحْمَة, رَحِيم, رَّحْمَٰن — grows from this one root image: life held and sustained inside a space of total, unearned care.
